cells.tense: Today you're the one holding the shape of what you keep alive, and it shows.
cells.ask: Pick the one thing you've carried long enough, and write down what's finished — one line, somewhere you'll see it, today. It gives you an edge to stop at.
cells.core:
On an ordinary day you look at what you're holding and you can feel the whole shape of it — what needs the most, what can wait, what's already done — and you act from that, not from the loudest thing in front of you. Two demands pull at once and you keep both moving without grinding yourself down, which is rarer than it sounds. What you keep alive comes out steady because you've been steady with it.

The work now is letting one thing be finished, in your hands, on paper. When you've got a place to stop, what's complete can be set down and what's next gets your full weight instead of the leftover. Write it down and let it count.
cells.sheetLine: You know the shape of what you carry, and you carry it on purpose.

cells.tense: Your attention has gone ahead to what this could turn into, and you're living there before it's here.
cells.ask: Leave one thing alone for a day — one thing you're tempted to adjust — and write down what it does on its own. It shows you which parts actually need your hands.
cells.core:
On an ordinary day you watch what you're building and you let it take its own shape, because you've done the part that was yours. You can look at something half-grown and feel satisfied with where it's got to rather than reaching for the next rung.

But lately you keep working ahead of the thing itself — adjusting, planning, fixing what hasn't happened yet, because you can see the pattern and the pattern wants the shape you've already got in mind. Some of that care is real and some of it is you holding on. Leaving one piece alone for a day is how you find out which one it was, and what's left when you stop.

cells.tense: You're still standing at a door you walked through a while back, tending what's behind it.
cells.ask: Say one sentence about what you're growing to someone who'd understand it — what it is, and that it's yours. It gives the work a voice, and a voice is harder to lose.
cells.core:
The clear version of this is simple: you can point at what you're growing and tell someone what it is and why it matters, in a few plain words, without dressing it up. You know how it works and what it needs, and you can say so out loud.

As it stands, all of that stays inside. You can see how everything fits together, clearly, better than most — and you don't hand that out, so nothing you grow gets confirmed by anyone but you. The clarity is real; it's the saying of it that stopped. One sentence to one person is how that starts again.

cells.tense: You're already keeping something alive, and you talk about it as though it were running without you.
cells.ask: Name one thing you set up and keep running, and write that name in your own hand. It marks the keeping as yours to hold or hand on.
cells.core:
Good keeping here looks like knowing what you're holding — seeing the shape of it, naming what it needs, doing the small consistent things that keep it alive. You do those things, most days, without ceremony.

What you don't do is own it. You call the care a habit, the upkeep just what's needed, the pattern something you happened to notice. But you are in fact picking what gets fed and what gets let be, and the credit for that goes to no one in particular, which means it can't be handed on either. Naming one thing as yours is what makes it yours to give.
